summary: Describes early DNS security extensions that add cryptographic digital signatures so resolvers and applications can verify DNS data integrity and authenticity. It was replaced by RFC 2535.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2065 was the first attempt to make the Domain Name System trustworthy. It puts digital signatures into DNS records, so a resolver can check that an answer really came from the zone it claims to come from, and adds a way to prove that a name does not exist rather than simply being absent.

subtitle: The original DNSSEC design: signed DNS records, published keys, and a way to prove a name is not there.

tldr.problem: The DNS is a critical part of the Internet and has no strong mechanism for data integrity or authentication, so anything it says can be forged or altered in transit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three record types to DNS: KEY, which publishes a public key, SIG, which carries a signature over other records, and NXT, which proves that a name or a type does not exist. Two header bits tell a resolver when a server has verified data.
tldr.outcome: A resolver that trusts one key can check the rest for itself, and existing servers that do not understand the new types can still carry the traffic. This design was replaced by RFC 2535.

facts.label: Signature times
facts.value: seconds since 1 January 1970, GMT, ignoring leap seconds

today: RFC 2065 has been obsoleted by RFC 2535, so it is no longer a current standards document. It was published in January 1997 as a Proposed Standard, and it updated RFCs 1034 and 1035.

sections.title: What the Extensions Provide
sections.content:
The DNS has become a critical operational part of the Internet infrastructure, yet it has no strong security mechanism to assure data integrity or authentication. The extensions described here provide those services to security aware resolvers or applications through the use of cryptographic digital signatures. The signatures are included in secured zones as resource records, and security can still be provided even through DNS servers that are not themselves security aware.

The extensions also provide for the storage of authenticated public keys in the DNS, which can support a general public key distribution service as well as DNS security itself. The stored keys let security aware resolvers learn the authenticating key of zones beyond those they are initially configured with, and keys associated with DNS names can be retrieved to support other protocols. Provision is made for a variety of key types and algorithms. In addition, the extensions provide for the optional authentication of DNS protocol transactions.

Three services are distinguished: key distribution, data origin authentication and integrity, and transaction and request authentication. Two things are deliberately not provided. It is part of the design philosophy of the DNS that the data in it is public and that the DNS gives the same answers to all inquirers, so no attempt has been made to include access control lists or other means of differentiating inquirers. And no effort has been made to provide confidentiality for queries or responses, although that service may be available through IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS is open by design: everyone gets the same answers, and nothing in it is hidden. This RFC adds proof of origin without changing either of those things. It never hides traffic; it only lets a reader check that what it was told is genuine.

sections.title: The KEY Resource Record
sections.content:
The KEY resource record documents a key associated with a DNS name. It will be a public key, since only public keys are stored in the DNS. It can be the public key of a zone, of a host or other end entity, or of a user. A KEY record is, like any other record, authenticated by a SIG record, and security aware implementations must be designed to handle at least two simultaneously valid keys of the same type associated with a name. The type number for the KEY record is 25.

The data of a KEY record is a flags field, a protocol octet, an algorithm number and the public key itself. The flags and the algorithm must be examined before any data that follows the algorithm octet, because they control the format and even whether there is any following data. The format of the public key itself depends on the algorithm.

The public key belongs to the object named in the owner name, and that name may refer to up to three different kinds of thing: a zone, a host or other end entity, and the mapping of a user or account into a DNS name. The flags say which of these roles applies. An appropriate zone KEY record must occur at the apex node of a secure zone and at every leaf node that is a delegation point. Overloading one name for several of these roles is discouraged, as is using one key for several things, because the use of a zone key for something else usually requires keeping the private key on line and so makes it more exposed.

The flags field carries several separate bits. Bits 0 and 1 form a type field: bit 0 set prohibits the key for authentication, bit 1 set prohibits it for confidentiality, and both zero permits both. DNS security uses keys for authentication only, but the confidentiality flag is provided for use in other protocols. When both bits are one the record carries the no key value, there is no key information, and the record stops after the algorithm octet. By using the no key value, a signed KEY record can authentically assert that, for example, a zone is not secured. Bit 2 is the experimental bit: when it is zero, security based on the key is mandatory, so a zone whose key has the bit off should be assumed secured and any answer saying otherwise is bogus. Bits 3 and 4 are reserved and must be zero. Bit 5 marks a key belonging to a user or account, bit 6 a key belonging to a non-zone entity such as a host, and bit 7 a zone key, which is the key used for data origin authentication. Bit 8 is reserved to IPsec, bit 9 to email security multiparts, bits 10 and 11 must be zero, and bits 12 to 15 are the signatory field, which says the key may sign records or updates of the same name.

The protocol octet says whether the key is also valid for another protocol. Values from 1 to 191 are assigned by IANA, the values from 192 to 254 are for experimental use under bilateral agreement, 0 means the key is valid for no protocol beyond those in the flag field, and 255 means it is valid for every assigned protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A KEY record publishes a public key and says what it is for: signing a whole zone, signing for one machine, or belonging to one user. The flags also let a zone say, in a signed record, that it has no key at all, which is how a resolver learns that a zone is deliberately not signed.

sections.title: The SIG Resource Record
sections.content:
The SIG, or signature, resource record is the fundamental way data is authenticated in the secure DNS, and the heart of the security provided. A SIG record unforgably authenticates other records of a particular type, class and name, and binds them to a time interval and to the signer's domain name, using cryptographic techniques and the signer's private key. The signer is frequently the owner of the zone from which the record originated.

The data of a SIG record holds the type of the records being covered, the algorithm used, a count of labels, the original time to live, the time the signature expires, the time it was signed, a key footprint, the signer's name and the signature itself. The type number for the SIG record is 24. The MD5/RSA algorithm described in the RFC is number 1; numbers 2 to 252 are available for assignment; 254 is reserved for private use, where the signature area begins with a length byte and an object identifier naming the private algorithm; 253 is the expiration date algorithm, used when the dates are wanted without any actual security, and its signature field is null; and 0 and 255 are reserved.

The labels octet counts the labels in the original owner name, not counting the null label for root and not counting any initial asterisk for a wildcard. If a secured retrieval is the result of wildcard substitution, the resolver has to use the original form of the name when verifying the signature, and this field helps it find that form. If the retrieved name is longer than the labels count, the record is a wildcard expansion; if it is shorter, the SIG record must be considered corrupt and ignored. The maximum number of labels allowed in the current DNS is 127.

The original time to live is included in the signed data to avoid the authentication problems caching servers would cause by decrementing the real time to live, and the security problems unscrupulous servers could cause by manipulating it. The original value is protected by the signature while the current one is not, and it must be restored into the covered records when the signature is verified, which implies that all records of a particular type, name and class must start with the same time to live. The signature is valid until the expiration time, an unsigned number of seconds since the start of 1 January 1970 GMT ignoring leap seconds, and a record whose expiration precedes its signing time must be treated as corrupt. The key footprint is a 16-bit quantity that helps pick between several applicable keys and gives a quick check that a key about to be used may be the right one.

Signatures are made with a private key that belongs to the zone rather than to the servers holding copies of the data, so compromising one server or even all the servers for a zone need not affect the assurance a resolver has. The expected implementation keeps the zone private key off line and re-signs all the records in the zone periodically. A resolver can learn the public key of a zone by reading it from DNS or by having it statically configured, but to learn it reliably from DNS the key itself must be signed, so the resolver must be configured with at least the public key of one zone it can use to authenticate the others.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature record covers the other records with the same name and type. It says who signed, when, until when the signature counts, and carries the signature itself. The key that made it is the zone's key, kept off the servers, so seizing a server does not let an attacker forge answers.

sections.title: Proving a Name Does Not Exist
sections.content:
The signature mechanism gives strong authentication to records that exist in a zone, but on its own it says nothing about the non-existence of a name or of a type for an existing name. That gap is filled by the NXT, or next, record, which authentically asserts a range of non-existent names in a zone and the non-existence of types for the name just before that range.

The NXT record is used to securely indicate that records with an owner name in a certain name interval do not exist in a zone, and to indicate which zone signed record types are present for an existing name. Its owner name is an existing name in the zone, and its data is a next name and a type bit map. The presence of the record means that generally no name between its owner name and the name in its data area exists, and that no other zone signed types exist under its owner name. This implies a canonical ordering of all domain names in a zone, with labels sorted as unsigned left justified octet strings, the absence of an octet sorting before a zero octet, and upper case letters treated as lower case.

The last NXT in a zone would need a next name covering the whole remainder of the name space, which is not obvious, so the name space is treated as circular and the zone name goes in the data of the last NXT. The NXT records for a zone should be calculated automatically and added by the same off-line process that signs the zone, and their time to live should not exceed the zone minimum.

The data of an NXT record is a domain name followed by a bit map, and the type number for the NXT record is 30. The bit map is one bit per record type present for the owner name, similar to the socket bit map. A one bit indicates at least one record of that type is present, a zero indicates none, and bits beyond the end of the map are assumed to be zero. The bit for NXT itself is always on, so the minimum map length is four octets.

A NXT record and its signature are returned in the authority section along with the error, if the server is security aware, which is a change to the existing standard, which contemplates only NS and SOA records in that section. Because a zone with a complete set of NXT records always yields at least one signed record in any reply, a query for any name and type to a security aware server always has something signed in the answer. NXT records do not appear in zone master files, since they can be derived from the rest of the zone. The RFC's example: in a zone foo.tld holding big, medium, small and tiny, a query for huge.foo.tld returns an error whose authority section carries an NXT record at big.foo.tld pointing at medium.foo.tld, together with the NXT's own signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing what exists is only half the job. A resolver also needs to be able to prove that a name is absent, because otherwise a fake answer that simply omits it looks identical to a real one. The NXT record covers a whole range of names at once and says which types do exist at the name before the range.

sections.title: Resolving Securely and the AD and CD Bits
sections.content:
Resolving authentic data involves starting with one or more trusted public keys for one or more zones. With trusted keys, a resolver willing to perform cryptography can progress securely through the secure zone structure to the zone of interest. Data stored at a security aware server is categorised in four ways. Authenticated means the data has a valid signature under a key traceable through a chain of zero or more signature and key records to a key configured at the resolver in its boot file. Pending means there are no authenticated signatures and at least one more signature the resolver is still trying to authenticate. Insecure means the data can never be authenticated or found bad, because it is in or was reached through a non-secured zone. Bad is a fourth transient state meaning that all signature checks have explicitly failed; such data is not retained at a security aware server.

Two previously unused bits are allocated from the must-be-zero field of the query and response header. The AD bit, for authentic data, indicates in a response that the data included has been verified by the server providing it. The CD bit, for checking disabled, indicates in a query that non-verified data is acceptable to the resolver sending it. Both bits are zero in old servers and resolvers, so the responses of old servers are not flagged as authenticated, and queries from resolvers that are not security aware do not assert the CD bit and so are answered by security aware servers only with authenticated data. Aware resolvers must not trust the AD bit unless they trust the server they are talking to and either have a secure path to it or use DNS transaction security.

Any security aware resolver willing to do cryptography should assert the CD bit on all queries, which reduces latency by letting security aware servers answer before they have settled the validity of the data. Security aware servers never return Bad data. For resolvers that are not security aware, or for aware resolvers that cleared the CD bit, a security aware server must return only Authenticated or Insecure data with the AD bit set. It may return Pending data to an aware resolver that asked for it by clearing the AD bit, and the AD bit must not be set unless every record in the response is either Authenticated or Insecure.

Starting from trusted keys for a zone, a resolver should be able to retrieve signed keys for its subzones and, unless the zone is the root, for its superzone. Every authoritative secure zone server must also include the key record for its superzone, signed by the secure zone through a key file directive, which makes it possible to climb the tree of zones when starting below the root. A secure subzone is indicated by a key record with non-null key information appearing alongside the NS records for that subzone. A resolver should keep track of how many successive secure zones it has traversed, because the lower that distance number, the greater its confidence; data configured through a boot file directive gets a distance of zero. If a query turns up different data for the same query with different distance values, the one with the larger value is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver keeps one or more keys it already trusts and works down the tree of zones, checking each key it picks up along the way. Two bits in the query header let it say whether it is in a hurry, and let the server say whether the answer has been checked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is careful about the limits of what it provides. At most, these extensions guarantee the validity of the resource records, including key records, retrieved from the DNS. They do not solve other security problems. Having high confidence in the IP address retrieved for a host name, for example, does not stop someone substituting an unauthorised host at that address, or capturing packets sent to that address and falsely responding with packets apparently from it. Any reasonably complete security system will require the protection of many additional facets of the Internet.

One operational requirement follows from the design. Coordinated interpretation of the time fields in signature records requires reasonably consistent time on the hosts running the extensions. If a time synchronisation protocol such as the Network Time Protocol is used, it must be used securely, so that time cannot be spoofed. Otherwise a host could have its clock turned back and then believe old signature and key records which were valid but no longer are.
sections.plainLanguage: These extensions prove that DNS answers are genuine. They do not prove that the machine behind an address is honest, and they depend on the clock being right, because a signature record carries the times it was made and expires.

viz.caption: THE THREE NEW DNS RECORD TYPES

items.title: KEY, type 25
items.text: Publishes a public key for a name, and says with its flags whether the key belongs to a zone, a host or a user, or whether there is no key at all.

items.title: SIG, type 24
items.text: Carries a digital signature over other records of the same name and type, with the times it was made and expires and the name of the signer.

items.title: NXT, type 30
items.text: Covers a range of names that do not exist in a zone, and lists which record types do exist at the name just before that range.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STATES A SECURITY AWARE SERVER KEEPS DATA IN

cells: The data has a valid signature under a key traceable through a chain of signature and key records to a key configured at the resolver.
There are no authenticated signatures yet, and at least one more signature the resolver is still trying to authenticate.
The data can never be authenticated and cannot be found bad, because it is in or was reached through a non-secured zone.
All signature checks have explicitly failed on the data. Such data is not retained at a security aware server.

viz.caption: THE FIXED PART OF A KEY RECORD'S DATA

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Says what the key may be used for: the key type bits, the experimental bit, the zone, entity and user bits, the IPsec and email bits, and the signatory field.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: Whether the key is also valid for another protocol. 0 means none, 255 means all assigned protocols.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Which algorithm the key belongs to. The MD5/RSA algorithm is number 1.
